food.text: Spirit Cave in Thailand was occupied by Hoabinhian hunter-gatherers between about 9000 and 5500 BCE, and was once presented as evidence for the early development of agriculture in Southeast Asia. That claim is now considered outdated by archaeologists.
The people who lived at Spirit Cave ate shellfish and hunted wild animals for meat. They also gathered plants from twenty-two different genera, using them as food, condiments or stimulants.

Researcher Viet studied the Da But site in Vietnam, which dates from about the fifth to sixth millennium BCE. He found that the Hoabinhian people there mainly ate mountainous shellfish, nuts and fruit.
Asian rice had been domesticated in China thousands of years earlier. It reached Austroasiatic and Kra-Dai speaking peoples in Mainland Southeast Asia and southern China by about 5000 years ago.

Archaeologist Chester Gorman passed sediment from Spirit Cave through a fine mesh screen, the first time this had been done at a prehistoric site in Thailand. This revealed many small animal bones, and every layer of the site contained remains of sambar deer.

Freshwater bivalves eaten by the people of Spirit Cave were likely gathered during the dry season. Low water levels at that time of year would have made the shellfish easy to collect, according to Gorman's original interpretation.

Nearby Steep Cliff Cave was also occupied by Hoabinhian hunter-gatherers, from about 5500 to 3500 BCE. This account, from Sing C. Chew, adds to the picture of hunting and gathering across the wider Spirit Cave region.

Besides sambar deer, some layers at Spirit Cave held bones of pigs, small deer, and monkeys such as langurs, macaques and gibbons. Squirrels, palm civets, martens, otters, jungle cats and badgers were also found, showing how varied Hoabinhian hunting was.

In 1972, researcher W. G. Solheim claimed that the inhabitants of Spirit Cave had an 'advanced knowledge of horticulture.' He cautioned, however, that the plant specimens found might simply be wild species gathered from the surrounding countryside.
Ceramic technology is not evident at Spirit Cave until after 6800 BCE, well after the site's earliest occupation by Hoabinhian hunter-gatherers.
At the Da But site, Hoabinhian people also ate an as-yet-unnamed species of freshwater clam from the genus Corbicula. This species is known to live in swampy areas and lakes.
Radiocarbon dating of four freshwater crab remains from Spirit Cave placed them between about 7850 and 6500 BCE. Oddly, their ages appeared in reverse order from the layers in which they were found.

At Da But in Vietnam, Viet observed that Hoabinhians mostly ate mountainous shellfish, nuts and fruit. The site even shows a new shellfish species they consumed: an as-yet-unnamed freshwater clam of the genus Corbicula.

art.text: The earliest known Filipino arts are rock arts, and the oldest are the Angono Petroglyphs, made in the Neolithic age between 6000 and 2000 BC. The carvings were possibly used in an ancient healing practice for sick children.
Vietnamese art has a long history, and its earliest examples date back to the Stone Age, around 8,000 BCE.

Vietnamese art is counted among the oldest of the Southeast Asian cultures. Its heritage reaches back to prehistoric times and eventually grew to include silk painting, sculpture, pottery, architecture, music, dance and theatre.
Art in Vietnam is described as having first appeared as clay pots made during the Stone Age. It is estimated that Vietnamese art began when indigenous groups started creating pottery.
Pottery from around 8000 BCE has been found at Bắc Sơn in Vietnam. It was made from clay and was largely basic, lacking artistic flair in its beginnings.

As early as 10,000 years ago, Hoabinhian settlers from Mainland Southeast Asia had developed a tradition and culture of distinct artefact and tool production. It is among the earliest crafting traditions named in the region's history.
Art in Vietnam was first introduced as clay pots created during the Stone Age. It is estimated that Vietnamese art began when indigenous groups started making pottery.
Vietnamese pottery began plainly at Bắc Sơn, but things changed when the Neolithic era arrived. Pottery and ceramics then started to develop rapidly, and they began to show signs of decoration.

science.text: Starting around 10,000 BCE, hunter-gatherers across Southeast Asia began making a distinctive kind of stone tool called Hoabinhian. Archaeologists describe it as a lithic techno-complex dated to c. 10,000–2000 BCE. How its technology changed over time is still poorly understood.

Around 5,500 years ago (3500 BCE), the Austronesian expansion began from Taiwan and coastal southern China. Thanks to their early invention of ocean-going outrigger boats and voyaging catamarans, Austronesians rapidly colonised Island Southeast Asia. They later spread as far as Polynesia and Madagascar.

Bananas and plantains were first domesticated in Southeast Asia, most likely in Papua New Guinea. They were later re-domesticated in Africa, possibly as early as 5,000 years ago. Asian yams and taro were also cultivated in Africa.

The Hoabinhian is named after Hòa Bình, Vietnam, where its cave and rock shelter sites were first described. Similar stone tools and flaked cobble artefacts, appearing around 10,000 BP, were later documented in Terengganu, Sumatra, Thailand, Laos, Myanmar, Cambodia and Yunnan. The artefacts varied in quality and nature depending on local environment and resources.
Research in 2003 suggests that in regions such as the Southeast Asian peninsula, the shift from hunting and gathering to farming was not a straight line. Instead, it was specific to each region.

Some Hoabinhian core tools are known as Sumatraliths. They were made by completely flaking one side of a pebble. Grinding stones were also made on rounded pebbles, usually found together with iron oxide.
The Bacsonian is often regarded as a variation of the Hoabinhian, dated to c. 8000–4000 BCE. It is marked by a higher frequency of edge-grounded cobble artifacts than earlier Hoabinhian tools.

In 1972, W. G. Solheim wrote in Scientific American that the people of Spirit Cave had an advanced knowledge of horticulture. He suggested ceramic technology was invented at 13,000 BCE, although Spirit Cave has no ceramics until after 6800 BCE.

Analysis of individuals from the Con Co Ngua site in Thanh Hoa, Vietnam, about 6,200 years BP, used craniometric and dental nonmetric methods. It found them closest to people from Mai Da Dieu, then to present-day Vietnamese. They also resembled Late Pleistocene Southeast Asians.

Hà Văn Tấn found primitive flakes buried below Hoabinhian pebble tools at several Southeast Asian sites. He named this earlier flake technology Nguomian, after a large assembly of flakes at the Ngườm rock shelter in Thái Nguyên province, Vietnam.

culture.text: The Hoabinhian culture accounts for the first verified ritual burials in Southeast Asia. Its hunter-gatherer people left behind stone tools in caves and rock shelters, which is how we learn about their lives.

Around 10,000 years ago, Hoabinhian settlers developed a distinct tradition of making stone tools and flaked cobble artefacts. The style was first described in caves and rock shelters at Hòa Bình, Vietnam. Similar sites were later documented in Terengganu, Sumatra, Thailand, Laos, Myanmar, Cambodia and Yunnan.

During the Neolithic, several migrations shaped the region's peoples. Austroasiatic peoples populated Mainland Southeast Asia by land routes, while sea-borne Austronesian immigrants preferred to settle in Maritime Southeast Asia.

The Đa Bút site in Vietnam is a Neolithic cemetery distinguished by shell middens. It was excavated in the 1930s by Étienne Patte and has recently been carbon-dated to 5000 BC. Its people were hunter-gatherers and fishermen.

Some studies of Đa Bút found evidence of farming, both of livestock and of paddy rice. Other studies gave the site a slightly later date and found no evidence of food production at all. Archaeologists still disagree on how these early villagers fed themselves.

Đa Bút is the earliest culture in its region to post-date the Hoabinhian, so it marks the beginning of the second layer in the two-layer hypothesis. The site therefore stands at a turning point between older hunter-gatherer traditions and later ones.

More than 120 Hoabinhian sites are known in Vietnam. This concentration reflects intensive research there rather than the location of a centre of prehistoric Hoabinhian activity, so the culture was probably spread much more widely.
